n: The queen of Sheba, from southwest Arabia (modern Yemen) or possibly across the Red Sea, hears that Solomon’s fame is tied to the Lord. She comes to test his wisdom with riddles and difficult questions.

f.g: a wealthy kingdom in southern Arabia known for incense and spice trade.

n: She arrives with a grand caravan loaded with spices, gold, and gems—perhaps also on a trade mission, since Solomon’s Red Sea fleet affected her routes. She speaks openly about everything on her mind.

f.g: a retinue or caravan of attendants.

n: Solomon answers every question; nothing stumps him. His gift of wisdom from the Lord is on full display.
She observes not just his words but the visible fruits of his wisdom—his buildings and the order of his court.
The food, the seating of officials, the uniformed servants, the cupbearers, and the ascent to the temple overwhelm her. “No more spirit in her” means she was breathless with amazement.

f.g: food in general, not just flesh.

f.w: there was no more spirit in her

f.g: possibly ‘his burnt offerings’ (as in 2 Chronicles 9:4 margin); the Hebrew can be read either way.

n: She admits that the reports she heard at home were true.
She had been skeptical until she saw for herself. “The half was not told me” has become a proverb for something that surpasses its reputation.
She calls Solomon’s servants fortunate because they hear wise counsel every day.

Remarkably, this foreign queen praises Israel’s God. She recognizes that Solomon’s throne is a gift of the Lord’s love for Israel and exists to bring justice—a reminder of what kingship was meant to be.

f.g: fair rulings and right order in society.

n: Her gifts were lavish—about four tons of gold and an unequaled quantity of spices.

f.g: about 4 tons; a talent was roughly 75 pounds.

n: An aside about Hiram’s fleet: from Ophir it also brought precious almug wood and gems.

f.g: a rare fine wood, perhaps red sandalwood; called ‘algum’ in 2 Chronicles 2:8.

n: Solomon used the rare wood for supports (or railings) in the temple and palace, and for musical instruments for the temple singers.

f.g: stringed instruments, something like lyres or harps.

n: Solomon gives the queen everything she asks for, plus generous royal gifts, and she returns home. Ethiopian tradition later claimed a royal line descended from this visit, though the Bible says nothing of it.
Solomon’s yearly gold income was 666 talents—roughly 25 tons. The figure stresses his staggering wealth.

f.w: six hundred threescore and six talents

n: That was in addition to tolls from traders, tribute from Arabian rulers, and taxes from provincial governors.
He made two hundred large ceremonial shields covered in hammered gold, each using about fifteen pounds of gold.
Three hundred smaller gold shields hung in the “house of the forest of Lebanon,” a great hall named for its many cedar pillars. These shields would later be looted by Shishak of Egypt.

f.w: the house of the forest of Lebanon

n: Solomon’s throne was inlaid with ivory and overlaid with fine gold.
The throne had six steps, a rounded back, armrests, and a lion statue beside each armrest. Lions symbolized royal power and the tribe of Judah.
Twelve more lions lined the steps, perhaps representing the twelve tribes. No other kingdom had anything like it.
Even ordinary household vessels were gold. Silver was so common it was considered nearly worthless.
Solomon’s “ships of Tarshish”—large, long-distance trading vessels—made three-year voyages bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and exotic birds.

f.g: a type of large ocean-going ship; Tarshish was a distant port, perhaps in Spain.
the Hebrew word is uncertain; possibly peacocks or baboons.

n: This verse is the summit of Solomon’s glory. Yet readers of Deuteronomy notice that his gold, horses, and wives were exactly what a king was warned not to multiply.

f.w: exceeded all the kings of the earth

n: People from far and wide came to hear his wisdom—a wisdom the text credits to God, not to Solomon himself.

f.w: which God had put in his heart

n: Visitors brought gifts every year—essentially tribute paid by those who sought his favor.
Solomon assembled a large chariot army stationed in special cities and in Jerusalem—a contrast to the law’s caution against multiplying horses.
Silver was as common as stones and cedar as common as the sycamore-fig trees of the lowlands. The hyperbole paints an age of overflowing abundance.

f.g: the Shephelah, the low foothills west of Judah.
sycamore-fig, a common and less valuable tree.

n: Solomon’s merchants imported horses from Egypt and also from “Kue” (Cilicia, in modern Turkey). “Linen yarn” may be a misreading of the place name Kue.

f.g: Hebrew miqveh, possibly the place name ‘Kue’ (Cilicia).

n: Solomon’s agents acted as middlemen, selling chariots and horses to the Hittite and Aramean kings of the north. Israel prospered as a crossroads of trade.
